title: The Missing Witness
premise: Rosalind Whitlock, a night-shift taxi dispatcher with an uncanny ear for lies, has quietly solved three deaths the police ruled accidental. When a confession letter arrives postmarked the day after the funeral of his estranged mentor, Elias Vane, Rosalind realizes the letter was written by someone who knew it would reach him—and that the confession names a fourth death that hasn't happened yet. Following the letter's coded references through Vane's tangled estate, Rosalind uncovers a family fortune built on a stolen identity and a witness who was paid to disappear decades ago: himself, as a child. As the heirs close ranks to protect their inheritance, Rosalind must expose the original crime before the final heir silences him permanently, ending with Rosalind choosing to step out of the shadows, testify publicly, and dismantle the Whitlock-Vane legacy he unknowingly inherited.
about_author: August Quintana is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent eleven years transcribing testimony in cases where the truth never made it into the record. He writes mysteries about people who listen for a living.

chapters.title: The Frequency of Lies
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. On a slow night shift, Rosalind dispatches cabs while mentally replaying the three 'accidents' he solved from nothing but voice patterns and addresses. A call comes in from a number that's been disconnected for years. The emotional beat is quiet unease—the sense that his invisibility is fraying.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. A confession letter arrives, postmarked the day after Elias Vane's funeral, naming a murder no one reported and warning of one still to come. The handwriting is Vane's own. Rosalind feels grief curdle into suspicion; the beat is the first crack in his controlled, hidden life.

chapters.title: The Estate of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. He attends the reading of Vane's will, observing four heirs who perform grief badly. He's left only a brass key and a note: 'You already know why.' The heirs' cold courtesy signals they know who he is. Beat: dread beneath civility.

chapters.title: What the Dead Man Filed
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The brass key opens a storage locker of Vane's private files—decades of clippings, tapes, and a ledger of payments to someone called 'the Quiet Account.' Rosalind recognizes his own childhood address. Beat: vertigo as the case turns personal.

chapters.title: Night Routes
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Working his shift, he cross-references old cab logs with the ledger's payment dates, reconstructing a pattern of hush money spanning thirty years. A fellow dispatcher, Marta, notices his distraction and offers unexpected loyalty. Beat: fragile alliance against isolation.

chapters.title: The Heir Apparent
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. He interviews Julian Vane, eldest heir, under the pretext of settling Elias's unpaid cab fares. Julian's charm slips once, revealing contempt for anyone who might 'dig up the foundation.' Beat: Rosalind confirms the family knows more than they admit.

chapters.title: A Witness Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Digging into the original 1989 death at the heart of the estate, Rosalind finds the official record lists a witness who testified and then vanished. The witness's name was changed to protect a child. His hands shake. Beat: the horrifying dawning—he is the missing witness.

chapters.title: The Boy in the Tape
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. In the locker he plays a reel-to-reel recording: a child's voice giving testimony before it was buried. The voice is his own. Memory floods back—his mother's disappearance, the name change, Vane's lifelong 'kindness.' Beat: identity collapse and grief.

chapters.title: Paid to Disappear
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. He traces the Quiet Account: Vane was paid by the true culprit to relocate and silence the child witness, then spent decades guilt-taping everything. The confession letter was Vane's last act of conscience. Beat: complicated mourning for a man who both saved and used him.

chapters.title: Closed for Good
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. He approaches the police with the evidence and is politely stonewalled—the investigating officer from 1989 is now connected to the family by marriage. Beat: institutional rot revealed; power protecting itself across generations.

chapters.title: Marta's Warning
chapters.summary: POV Marta. She notices a luxury car idling outside the depot two nights running and tells Rosalind someone is watching him. Her fear on his behalf forces him to admit how deep he's in. Beat: warmth and terror intertwined; stakes become physical.

chapters.title: The Second Funeral
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. One of the four heirs, Aunt Corinne, dies suddenly—exactly the kind of death Rosalind has learned to read. The confession letter's predicted murder has happened. Beat: cold fury; the race is now explicitly against time.

chapters.title: Following the Money Down
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Following the estate's financial trail, he finds the fortune originates not in shipping but in a forged identity—a dead man's name laundered into legitimacy. Power built on a fiction. Beat: thematic crystallization of inheritance and corruption.

chapters.title: Julian's Offer
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Julian summons him and offers a share of the estate to walk away, framing silence as mercy: 'Elias bought you a quiet life. Honor it.' Rosalind refuses. Beat: temptation resisted; the cost of visibility named aloud.

chapters.title: The Disconnected Number
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The impossible phone call from chapter one recurs; tracing it through the depot's ancient switchboard, he reaches a retired operator who reveals who placed the calls—and that she was paid to forget. Beat: the conspiracy's web widens beyond the family.

chapters.title: House of Mirrors
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Breaking into the Vane house at night, he finds the original deed, photos of himself as a boy, and a second confession draft naming the killer outright—but pages are missing, torn away. Beat: so close, then robbed; despair sharpening resolve.

chapters.title: What Marta Knew
chapters.summary: POV Marta. She confesses she was hired at the depot years ago to keep an eye on Rosalind—for the family. Her betrayal-turned-devotion gives Rosalind the torn pages' location: Julian's safe. Beat: trust broken and rebuilt; the theme of purchased loyalty confronted.

chapters.title: The Safe and the Silence
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. With Marta's help he opens the safe during a memorial gathering, recovering the pages naming the killer: the family patriarch, alive and hidden, who staged his own death in 1989 and has been 'managing' the estate ever since. Beat: revelation and immediate danger.

chapters.title: Running Out of Night
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The patriarch's men corner Rosalind in the depot; Marta triggers the silent alarm, and a chase through the garage ends with Rosalind escaping with the pages but injured. Beat: climax begins—no more hiding, physically or otherwise.

chapters.title: The Last Dispatch
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. He uses the dispatch system to broadcast the whole story—recordings, ledger, confession—to every driver, journalist, and police scanner in the city simultaneously. The patriarch can't silence a thousand witnesses. Beat: triumphant inversion of his lifetime of listening in secret.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. In a reopened courtroom, Rosalind testifies under his birth name, spoken aloud for the first time in thirty years. The patriarch is arrested; the estate is frozen. Beat: catharsis—identity reclaimed through truth rather than inheritance.

chapters.title: Daylight Shift
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Weeks later, Rosalind takes a day job training new dispatchers, teaching them to hear what people hide. He visits Vane's grave without anger. Beat: resolution—invisibility traded for integrity; the listener finally speaks.
